newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's Krakow "dry" for Pope -- almost.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Krakow "dry" for Pope -- almost.

text.p: Hotel minibars were much in demand in Krakow when authorities banned liquor sales during Pope John Paul's three-day stay, leaving bartenders idly polishing glasses and politely saying "no" to thirsty pilgrims.
But there was no lack of ingenuity in circumventing the ban in the southern Polish city, where beer usually flows as briskly as the Vistula River that runs through it.
The prohibition applied to all liquor stores, pubs, restaurants and bars for one off-licence shop and a restaurant on the city outskirts - a daunting 30-minute taxi ride away.
"There will be no liquor sales until Monday evening when the Pope leaves Krakow," a disgruntled bartender in the Bambusowy pub in the old town district said.
"I can't even sell you a beer because breaking the ban would cost me a fine of 5,000 zlotys ($1,152)," he added.
Despite warm weather and thousands of pilgrims who came for the Pope's Sunday mass, customers were scarce in the usually bustling old town bars on Saturday night.

Romuald Styrylski of the "August" hotel bar estimates he might be losing 10,000 zlotys ($3,000) of sales every night of the prohibition which ends on Monday, the night before the Pope returns to Rome at the end of an 11-day trip.
"With all the pilgrims and tourists in town the bar would be bursting with people. As it is, they only come in, learn of the ban and go away," Styrylski said.
But some barmen quietly served gin tonics or margeritas to regular customers in tea cups to confuse city inspectors.
"I can't sell you beer, because it looks too obvious, but a stronger version of coke or juice can be arranged," said one bartender, who asked not to be named.
A loophole in the ban was a clause that alcohol could be served to private parties, such as wedding or birthday celebrations.
Many Krakow restaurants were closed to the public on Saturday night with signs reading 'private party' on the door. Nevertheless, uninvited guests managed to attend.
One vendor was giving beer away to advertise his brand.
"The prohibition concerns only sales of alcoholic beverges. It says nothing about giving them away," said a man operating a trolley with beer on tap.
"This is one of the most effective ways of advertising."
